title: What is an idiom? When cake means easy
description: Know every word in “a piece of cake” and still miss the meaning? Discover how an idiom works, with a slice of English that is not always dessert.

cover.alt: A slice of lemon cake on a cream plate beside an open notebook and a yellow pencil

practice: Look for another kind of link between words in Connections.

sources.name: Cambridge Dictionary — Idiom: the phrase and its meaning
Cambridge Dictionary — A piece of cake: something very easy to do

sections.title: The whole phrase has a job
sections.html:
An idiom is an expression whose meaning as a whole differs from the meanings of its individual words. Knowing each word is not always enough to work out what someone means.

Cambridge Dictionary describes this phrase-level meaning. The words arrive together with an established use of their own.

sections.title: Where is the cake?
sections.html:
Imagine a friend says, Putting up that tent was a piece of cake. You would not need to look for icing on the campsite.

A piece of cake is an informal way to describe something very easy to do. Our friend found the task easy; the tent has not become edible.

sections.title: Same words, different setting
sections.html:
Now imagine someone points at a plate and offers you a piece of cake. This time, reaching for a fork makes perfect sense.

The words are the same. The situation helps you decide whether the speaker means an actual slice or something easy. Reading only the word cake would miss that difference.

sections.title: A little language surprise
sections.html:
When a phrase seems odd, try looking it up as a whole expression. A dictionary entry can reveal a meaning that separate word definitions would not explain.

For another twist in English, meet words that can mean their own opposite. Or explore more ways words surprise us. The next puzzle might contain more than one kind of clue.
